rv.q: At two and a half blocky, discursive hours, the play is too novelistic and interior to succeed as a dynamic drama.
This is the kind of richly textured, novelistic play that reads beautifully on the page, but often stalls when brought to life.

Part of the pleasure of watching Sojourners lies in trying to figure out where the narrative is going; the good news is Udofia confidently guides them all to a denouement that is as surprising as it is satisfying.

With clear-eyed determination, Udofia has penned an immigrant's tale that is neither triumphal (like the wildly popular Hamilton) nor a complete refutation of the American Dream (like nearly every play by Eugene O'Neill).
Director Ed Sylvanus Iskandar has staged this deeply beautiful, complex new play with both compassion and humor.
Sojourners strongly if imperfectly fulfills that goal.
Given the promise of such an ambitious and potentially exciting project, one makes allowances for some of the awkwardness of this first production...
The cast, however, is unfailingly wonderful.
Sojourners is over written, slow-paced, and lacks clear plot points.
Udofia’s play cleverly touches on the variations of the American dream for everyone who feels like an outcast, whether they were born in the States or not...
Unfortunately, much of Udofia's detail-rich script plays as if it were a series of overlapping monologues, many of which repeat the same information.

Sojourners itself is too dependent on a stuttering dramatic urgency, internal monologues that tell instead of show, and artificially colorful characters to make a two and a half-hour sojourn with it especially inviting.

cn.t: Critics find Udofia's Nigerian immigrant drama features strong performances and compelling characters, but suffers from a static, overly talky structure that stretches its thin plot across an overlong running time.
